body: A woman is sitting in a supermarket car park with the engine off, because the shopping is already in the boot and she does not especially want to go home yet. Her son is four and is strapped in behind her, talking to the window. After a while the talking turns into singing. It is not a nursery rhyme. It is a line about the Lord being her portion, and he has one of the words wrong, and he sings it twice more with the wrong word and then loses interest in it entirely. She has never taught him that. The radio is on in the kitchen most mornings while she is making toast, and that is the whole of it.

Nobody in that car was teaching and nobody was studying. There was no book open, no hour set aside, nobody in the room whose job it was. And yet a sentence out of the Psalms had crossed from one generation into the next while somebody was buttering toast.

That is not a happy accident and it is not new. When a generation had to remember a warning long after the man delivering it was dead, Moses was not handed an outline. He was told to write a song, teach it to the children of Israel, and put it in their mouths.

The instruction is worth taking literally rather than admiring as an image. A song is engineering for getting words through time undamaged. Melody fixes the order of the phrases. Metre tells you how many syllables have gone missing when one goes astray. Rhyme catches the error and hands the word back. Prose has none of this. Prose is remembered as gist, and gist is precisely the part that goes first. The longest book in Scripture is a songbook, and it did not become the longest by accident — it is the part the people carried, because it was the part built to be carried.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations. Teaching and prayer have frequencies of their own. Music has most of the band, and that proportion was a decision rather than an accident.

Weighting a ministry that way costs something, because a song is far slower to build than a paragraph and far harder to correct once it has gone out. A wrong sentence can be rewritten this afternoon. A chorus that has lodged in ten thousand people takes a decade to shift, if it shifts at all. That cost is accepted here deliberately. Moses was told to teach Israel a song, not a lecture, because a song is what they would still have when everything else had been forgotten — and everything else always is.

That understanding has quietly gone out of the culture. Music is now treated as weather: something to set the temperature of a room, chosen by mood, skipped the moment the mood turns, and never expected to say anything a person will still be holding in twenty years. Churches feel it too, where the singing has become the warm part before the serious part and the serious part is always prose. Nobody decided this. It is simply what happens when a medium becomes abundant enough to carry no consequence, and the cost is that we have stopped putting anything important into the one container that was built to survive.

The band is arranged so a listener can find the register they need without hunting for it — the worship and praise formats together, country and gospel near one another, the hymn and heritage repertoire in its own stretch, the children’s frequencies grouped so that a parent can land on one without looking. Learn roughly where things sit and you can move about by feel. That is the skill a real dial teaches and a search box never can, because a search box can only hand back the thing you already knew to name.
None of which is an argument against preaching. It is an argument about what happens to preaching on the following Thursday.

Be fair to the sermon first, because it does things a song cannot. It can define a term, handle an objection, hold a hard passage open long enough to be understood, and correct an error out loud. A song can do none of that. But a sermon is heard once, in a building, at an hour somebody had to travel to, by a person sitting still on purpose, and every one of those conditions is a filter. What survives the week is usually not the argument. Ask almost any believer what Scripture they can say from memory and most of it arrives with a tune attached, and most of them cannot tell you when they learned it.
A sermon is heard once. A chorus is carried around all week.

In a care home on a Wednesday afternoon a man of eighty-six is being helped into a chair by a carer he has met perhaps forty times and does not recognise. He has very few words left. He has not managed his daughter’s name in a year and a half. Somebody has put a hymn on in the day room, quietly, because that is what goes on at that hour, and about halfway through the second verse his mouth starts moving. He gets the whole verse. He is not looking at anyone while he does it, and there is no particular expression on his face. When it finishes he goes back to where he was, and the carer, who is twenty-three and not religious, stands there holding a folded blanket.

Everything that had been filed in that man as knowledge was gone. What had been set to a tune was still exactly where somebody had put it, sixty years earlier, probably on a Sunday morning he was not paying much attention to.

The same property is what makes music dangerous, and it would be dishonest to sell the strength without naming the risk. A melody carries whatever is loaded onto it and does not check the load. A sentimental half-truth set to a good tune lodges just as deeply as a true line and is very much harder to get out again, because nobody argues with a chorus. They simply find themselves singing it. Music is not a safe medium. It is a strong one, which is a different thing.

Which is exactly why it deserves care rather than avoidance. A power this blunt does not become safer by being left to people who are not thinking about it, and there is a great deal of music written in the vocabulary of faith that rests on nothing whatever. The answer is not less singing. The answer is knowing what every song stands on, keeping that visible under the track rather than buried, and being willing to have it checked by anybody who cares to look.

So the question here was never whether to build another Christian streaming service. There are enough of those and most are perfectly good. The question was how to get the Word into the form that people actually keep. Music is that form. It was the form before there were books, it is the form the Psalms are in, and it is the form the apostles named when they told churches under real pressure to teach and admonish one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial, and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. No menu, no queue to build, and no decision to make before anything starts.

If you want somewhere to begin, begin at HM 305.40 — Torah Sings. It is where this article stops being an argument and becomes a description, because what it plays is Torah set to melody: the text itself, given a tune and a metre and sent out to be carried by people doing other things. It is the oldest strategy in Scripture running on a modern transmitter. Put it on in a kitchen for a fortnight, study nothing, and you will still find a line of the text going round with you on a Tuesday afternoon. That is not the station being clever. That is what the medium has always done, and it is the reason it was chosen.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a case. You do not have to agree with a word of the above to test it, and you do not need to set an hour aside, because that has never been how any of this works. Put HM 305.40 on this afternoon while you are doing something else, and then leave it alone. Give it a fortnight of ordinary mornings. Sooner or later somebody in your house will sing a line back at you with one of the words wrong, and you will know exactly where it came from.
